name: Carrie Nation
kicker: Hatchet-swinging temperance activist · Smashed Kansas saloons from 1900
briefing: Carrie Nation stood nearly six feet tall and believed God had called her to destroy saloons. Kansas had already banned alcohol, but illegal bars stayed open, so starting in 1900 she marched into them and smashed bottles, mirrors, and furniture, first with rocks and then with her famous hatchet. She was arrested about 30 times, paid her fines partly by selling souvenir hatchets, and died in 1911, nine years before national Prohibition began.
answerHtml: Carrie Nation (or Carry A. Nation; accept Carrie Amelia Moore Nation)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: This woman was born in Garrard County, Kentucky, in 1846, and she died in Leavenworth, Kansas, in 1911. Her gravestone in Belton, Missouri, says “She hath done what she could” and calls her “Faithful to the Cause of Prohibition.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this temperance activist who smashed Kansas saloons with a hatchet starting in 1900.

tossups.p: This woman’s first husband, Dr. Charles Gloyd, drank heavily and died about two years after their wedding; she blamed alcohol for ruining her marriage. Years later, she helped start a local chapter of a women’s temperance group in Medicine Lodge, Kansas.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this woman who later attacked saloons with a hatchet, starting in 1900.

tossups.p: In 1901, this woman’s second husband, a lawyer and minister named David, divorced her, saying she had deserted him. He was nineteen years older than she was. That same year, she began publishing a newspaper called _The Smasher’s Mail_.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this temperance activist famous for attacking saloons with a hatchet in Kansas.

tossups.p: In June 1900, this woman said a vision told her to go to Kiowa, Kansas, and smash its saloons. She rode there in a buggy loaded with rocks and bricks and threw them at the bottles and mirrors in the town’s illegal bars.
tossups.r: Later she began using a hatchet instead. For 10 points, name this Kansas temperance activist.

tossups.p: In December 1900, this woman smashed a large mirror and bottles at the bar of the Carey Hotel in Wichita, Kansas, and was arrested. Weeks later, she began carrying the tool that became her symbol.
tossups.r: That tool was a hatchet. For 10 points, name this temperance activist who smashed saloons in Kansas.

tossups.p: In 1901, this woman took her campaign to Topeka, the capital of Kansas, smashing saloons there and demanding that officials enforce the state’s ban on alcohol. Kansas had banned alcohol in its constitution since 1881.
tossups.r: She belonged to the Woman’s Christian Temperance Union. For 10 points, name this activist who attacked illegal bars with a hatchet.

tossups.p: This woman described herself as “a bulldog running along at the feet of Jesus, barking at what He doesn’t like.” She stood nearly six feet tall and believed God had chosen her to destroy saloons.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Kansas activist who smashed bars with a hatchet, beginning in 1900.

tossups.p: This woman was arrested about thirty times, and she paid her fines with money from lectures and appearances on vaudeville stages. Crowds came to hear the nearly six-foot-tall speaker describe her raids on bars.
tossups.r: She also sold souvenir pins shaped like a hatchet, her symbol. For 10 points, name this temperance activist from Kansas.

tossups.p: After Kansas banned alcohol in 1881, illegal saloons there were known as “joints,” and their owners as “jointists.” This woman began wrecking joints in 1900, arguing that because the bars broke the law, they could be destroyed.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this temperance activist who used a hatchet in her attacks.

tossups.p: This woman favored a spelling of her first name that turned her full name, with her middle initial, into a slogan, and she registered that version as a trademark. Her autobiography describes her visions and her raids on bars.
tossups.r: That spelling was “Carry.” For 10 points, name this temperance activist known for smashing saloons with a hatchet.

tossups.p: This woman gave her last public speech in Eureka Springs, Arkansas, in January 1911, collapsing after declaring, “I have done what I could.” She died that June in a hospital in Leavenworth, Kansas.
tossups.r: Her home in Eureka Springs was called Hatchet Hall. For 10 points, name this temperance activist who smashed saloons.

tossups.p: Douglas Moore, the composer of _The Ballad of Baby Doe_, wrote a 1966 opera about this woman that premiered at the University of Kansas. In real life, she lived for years in Medicine Lodge, Kansas, where her house is a National Historic Landmark.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this activist who attacked saloons with a hatchet, a member of the Woman’s Christian Temperance Union.

tossups.p: The temperance group this woman joined was founded in Cleveland in 1874 and was led for nearly twenty years by Frances Willard, whose “Do Everything” policy included women’s suffrage. This woman started a local chapter of that group in Kansas.
tossups.r: That group was the Woman’s Christian Temperance Union. For 10 points, name this member who smashed Kansas saloons with a hatchet.

tossups.p: A famous photograph shows this woman in a long dark dress, holding a Bible in one hand. She believed saloons ruined families by leaving wives and children poor while men spent their wages on drink.
tossups.r: In her other hand, she holds a hatchet. For 10 points, name this temperance activist who smashed Kansas saloons.

tossups.p: While the Anti-Saloon League lobbied lawmakers to ban alcohol, this woman took direct action, walking into illegal Kansas bars and destroying their stock and furniture. Nine years after her 1911 death, the 18th Amendment brought nationwide Prohibition.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this activist who swung a hatchet in her raids on saloons.

clues.t: Smashed saloons with a hatchet; she called her attacks “hatchetations”
Began wrecking illegal saloons in Kansas in 1900
A member of the Woman’s Christian Temperance Union (WCTU), founded in 1874
Fought for prohibition (banning alcohol); she died in 1911, nine years before the 18th Amendment took effect
Said a vision sent her to Kiowa, Kansas, where she smashed saloons with rocks and bricks (June 1900)
Lived in Medicine Lodge, Kansas, where she helped start a local WCTU chapter; her house there is a National Historic Landmark
Kansas had banned alcohol in its constitution since 1881, so the bars (“joints”) she attacked were illegal
Called herself “a bulldog running along at the feet of Jesus, barking at what He doesn’t like”
Arrested about 30 times; paid her fines with lecture and vaudeville money and sales of souvenir hatchet pins
Her first husband, Dr. Charles Gloyd, drank heavily and died about two years after their wedding
In December 1900, she smashed the bar of the Carey Hotel in Wichita
Famous photos show her holding a Bible in one hand and a hatchet in the other
Stood nearly six feet tall and believed God had chosen her to destroy saloons
Published a newspaper called _The Smasher’s Mail_ (1901)
Favored the spelling “Carry,” which made her full name a slogan, and registered that version as a trademark
Her second husband, David, a lawyer and minister 19 years older, divorced her in 1901, saying she had deserted him
In 1901, she smashed saloons in Topeka, the Kansas capital, and demanded that officials enforce the ban
Gave her last speech in Eureka Springs, Arkansas (January 1911), collapsing after saying “I have done what I could”; her home there was Hatchet Hall
Buried in Belton, Missouri; her stone reads “Faithful to the Cause of Prohibition, She Hath Done What She Could”
Born in Garrard County, Kentucky (1846); died in a hospital in Leavenworth, Kansas (1911)
Subject of a 1966 opera by Douglas Moore (composer of _The Ballad of Baby Doe_), first staged at the University of Kansas
Unlike the Anti-Saloon League (founded 1893), which lobbied lawmakers, she took direct action against bars
The WCTU was founded in Cleveland and led for nearly twenty years by Frances Willard, whose “Do Everything” policy included women’s suffrage

trap.title: Smasher or suffragist?
trap.body: Temperance and women’s rights clues overlap. Carrie Nation smashed saloons; Frances Willard led the Woman’s Christian Temperance Union for nearly twenty years; and Carrie Chapman Catt, another “Carrie,” led the final push for the 19th Amendment. Real tossups about the ban itself want Prohibition or the 18th Amendment, not her.
trap.fix: A hatchet, Kansas saloons, Kiowa, Medicine Lodge, and “hatchetations” mean Carrie Nation. Women’s suffrage and the 19th Amendment point to Catt or Susan B. Anthony, and “this law” or “this era” of banning alcohol means Prohibition. Her last name alone, “Nation,” is enough.
trap.line: Real answer line: Carrie Nation (or Carry A. Nation; accept Carrie Amelia Moore Nation)
